hints: Look closely at cell X on the top scale, how many small eyepiece graticule divisions does it cover from its left edge to its right edge?
Look at the lower calibration image, how many eyepiece divisions line up exactly with 0.2 mm on the stage micrometer, and what does that make 1 division equal to in micrometres?
walkthrough:
**Measure cell X in eyepiece units**

First, we never measure cells directly in mm. We count how big it looks in eyepiece divisions.

Cell X stretches from about 25 to about 36 on the graticule. That is 11 small divisions.

**Calibrate one eyepiece division**

Now swap to the stage micrometer, which has a real scale in mm. We line up the two scales starting at 0.

30 eyepiece divisions line up exactly with 0.2 mm on the stage.

Convert to micrometres first:
$$0.2 \text{ mm} = 0.2 \times 1000 = 200 \, \mu m$$

So:
$$1 \text{ eyepiece division} = \frac{200 \, \mu m}{30} = 6.67 \, \mu m$$

**Calculate the real diameter**

Just multiply the size in divisions by the value of one division.
$$\text{diameter} = 11 \times 6.67 \, \mu m \approx 73.3 \, \mu m$$

That rounds to about $73 \, \mu m$, which is option C.

options.A: Too tiny by a factor of 10,000. This comes from mixing up mm and micrometres. Remember $1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \, \mu m$, not 1,000,000.
options.B: Close but a little small. This uses 10 eyepiece divisions instead of the full 11 divisions that cell X actually covers.
options.C: Correct. 11 eyepiece divisions multiplied by 6.67 micrometres per division gives about 73 micrometres.
options.D: Ten times too big. This comes from using 0.2 mm as 2000 micrometres instead of 200 micrometres when calibrating.
